Title: MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution
Problem addressed: Tuple-at-a-time (Volcano) engines use modern CPUs poorly (low instructions per cycle) on analytical queries.
Method: Vectorised execution: each operator processes a small, cache-resident vector of column values in a tight loop.
Key result: One to two orders of magnitude faster than earlier systems on TPC-H 100 GB.
Limitation / gap: Single research prototype from 2005; predates wide SIMD, GPUs and Apache Arrow.

Title: Rethinking SIMD Vectorization for In-Memory Databases
Problem addressed: Database operators used SIMD only in ad hoc ways.
Method: General SIMD designs (gathers/scatters) for selection scans, hash tables, partitioning, sorting and joins.
Dataset: Synthetic micro-benchmarks on Xeon Phi and mainstream CPUs
Key result: Up to an order of magnitude faster than earlier scalar and vector versions.
Limitation / gap: Operator-level study; not measured inside complete, end-user engines.

Authors, year: Kersten, Leis, Kemper, Neumann, Pavlo, Boncz (2018)
Title: Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Compiled and Vectorized Queries But Were Afraid to Ask
Problem addressed: It was unclear whether vectorisation or data-centric code generation gives faster queries.
Method: Implements both models in one test system with the same algorithms and data structures.
Key result: Both are efficient: vectorisation hides cache-miss latency better, compilation needs fewer CPU instructions.
Limitation / gap: C++ research engines; does not cover Python-facing libraries.

Title: DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database
Problem addressed: No in-process (embedded) database existed for analytics, as SQLite does for transactions.
Method: Embedded columnar engine with vectorised execution, demonstrated against other data management tools.
Key result: Shows an analytical engine can run as a library inside the host process.
Limitation / gap: Demo paper: no breakdown of where its speed comes from (execution model vs cores).

Title: A Study of the Fundamental Performance Characteristics of GPUs and CPUs for Database Analytics
Problem addressed: Reported GPU speed-ups (2x to 100x) may come from weak CPU baselines.
Method: Performance models plus Crystal, a library of GPU routines, compared with optimised CPU code.
Key result: GPU about 25x faster than CPU on the benchmark, largely explained by memory bandwidth.
Limitation / gap: Needs data-centre GPUs with data already in GPU memory.

Title: Database Systems on GPUs
Problem addressed: No consolidated view of how GPU database systems are designed.
Method: Survey of GPU data layouts, operators, query processing, optimisation and systems.
Key result: GPU-optimised designs give significant gains over CPU designs for main-memory databases.
Limitation / gap: Survey only; no new measurements on commodity hardware.

Title: Maximizing Persistent Memory Bandwidth Utilization for OLAP Workloads
Problem addressed: Can persistent memory (Intel Optane) replace costly DRAM for analytical queries?
Method: Systematic bandwidth study of PMem, then analytical queries run from PMem.
Key result: Average query slowdown of only 1.66x vs DRAM; seven best practices for using PMem.
Limitation / gap: Intel has since discontinued Optane, which limits practical use.

Title: Photon: A Fast Query Engine for Lakehouse Systems
Problem addressed: JVM-based Spark execution is slow on raw, uncurated lakehouse data.
Method: Native C++ vectorised engine that adapts to each batch of data at run time.
Key result: About 3x average (over 10x max) speed-up over the previous Databricks Runtime; audited TPC-DS record.
Limitation / gap: Proprietary cloud system; results cannot be reproduced by students.

Title: Velox: Meta's Unified Execution Engine
Problem addressed: Many engines at Meta re-implement the same execution logic.
Method: Open-source C++ library of reusable, vectorised execution components.
Dataset: Meta production workloads (Presto, Spark and others)
Key result: Integrated into more than a dozen Meta systems, improving efficiency and consistency.
Limitation / gap: Aimed at engine builders; no single-machine comparison with dataframe tools.

Title: Orchestrating Data Placement and Query Execution in Heterogeneous CPU-GPU DBMS
Problem addressed: Data larger than GPU memory must be split between CPU and GPU.
Method: Mordred: data-aware caching plus co-execution of a query on CPU and GPU.
Key result: Caching up to 3x better than the best traditional policy; an order of magnitude faster than existing GPU DBMSs.
Limitation / gap: Requires a GPU and a research prototype.

Title: Query Processing on Heterogeneous CPU/GPU Systems
Problem addressed: How to split work between CPU and GPU and overcome the data-transfer bottleneck.
Method: Survey with a classification scheme for heterogeneous query processors.
Key result: Categorises existing CPU/GPU systems and lists open research problems.

Title: A Deep Dive into Common Open Formats for Analytical DBMSs
Problem addressed: Unclear how common open formats perform inside analytical DBMSs.
Method: Detailed empirical evaluation of three widely used open formats.
Key result: Parquet is mostly used only as storage; Arrow's unencoded layout suits vectorised execution.
Limitation / gap: Storage-focused; does not time group-by/join in dataframe libraries.

Authors, year: Zeng, Hui, Shen, Pavlo, McKinney, Zhang (2023)
Title: An Empirical Evaluation of Columnar Storage Formats
Problem addressed: Parquet and ORC were designed in the early 2010s; hardware and workloads have changed.
Method: Deep dive into format internals plus a benchmark that stress-tests speed and size.
Dataset: Benchmark generator modelled on real-world data distributions
Key result: Recommends dictionary encoding by default and favouring decoding speed over compression ratio.
Limitation / gap: Formats only; does not measure query-engine compute.

Title: GPU Database Systems Characterization and Optimization
Problem addressed: Bottlenecks and resource use of GPU databases are poorly understood.
Method: Cross-stack performance analysis of four GPU databases, including Crystal and TQP.
Key result: GPUs are often under-used; tuning and GPU partitioning improve latency and concurrent throughput.
Limitation / gap: Data-centre GPUs; no comparison with CPU dataframe libraries.

Title: Robust External Hash Aggregation in the Solid State Age
Problem addressed: Group-by speed falls off a cliff when intermediate results exceed RAM.
Method: Unified memory management and a spillable page layout in DuckDB's parallel hash aggregation.
Key result: Degrades gracefully beyond memory while staying competitive in memory.
Limitation / gap: Out-of-memory focus; SIMD vs thread contributions not separated.

Title: Apache Arrow DataFusion: A Fast, Embeddable, Modular Analytic Query Engine
Problem addressed: Building a fast analytical engine from scratch is costly.
Method: Modular Rust engine with Arrow as its in-memory format; vectorised and multi-threaded.
Key result: Shows a modular, extensible Arrow-native engine need not sacrifice performance.
Limitation / gap: Not compared with Pandas-style data science workflows.

Title: Saving Private Hash Join
Problem addressed: Join speed drops sharply when the build side does not fit in RAM.
Method: Adaptive external hash join in a unified buffer pool, run-time compression and dynamic memory sharing.
Key result: Avoids the performance cliff; shipped in DuckDB v1.2.0.
Limitation / gap: Out-of-memory focus; in-memory execution gains not isolated.

Authors, year: Mozzillo, Zecchini, Gagliardelli, Aslam, Bergamaschi, Simonini (2025)
Title: Evaluation of Dataframe Libraries for Data Preparation on a Single Machine
Problem addressed: Data scientists lack rigorous comparisons of Pandas and its alternatives.
Method: Experimental comparison of Pandas, PySpark, Modin, Polars, cuDF, Vaex and DataTable.
Key result: Pandas best for small data; Polars when data fits in RAM; cuDF fastest when a GPU is available.
Limitation / gap: Does not separate execution-model gains from multi-core gains.
